Elif kept the sketchbook under her biology textbook, the way other kids hid phones. In the Berlin flat above her father's bakery, the plan had been said so often it sounded like a fact: Elif would study medicine, the first doctor in the family.
'Just do the biology course,' Tuan said at lunch. 'Draw on weekends. Easier than a war.'

Her mother turned the pages slowly. At the last one, a girl carrying bread up the stairs, she stopped. 'This is our staircase.'
'Yes.'
'Tell me more,' her mother said, and pushed the tea aside.

At the Thursday cattle market outside the kasba, Wasim sold three goats before noon and felt nothing. Last night his son Faiz, fifteen, had pushed away the mutton curry and said quietly, 'Abbu, I don't want to eat meat anymore. And I don't want to trade goats.'
Wasim had walked out without a word.
On the bus home he sat beside Mahima, the schoolteacher from the next lane. 'Three generations,' he said. 'And he looks at our work like it's wrong.'
'Did you ask him why?'
He hadn't.
That evening he found Faiz feeding the young goat by the shed. Wasim sat on an upturned bucket. 'Tell me. From the start. I'll listen first.'
Faiz talked for a long time, about the goats' faces, about a veterinary course in the city. Wasim felt fear in his chest, and a strange pride too, at how carefully his boy had thought.

The offer letter from the bank arrived today. Permanent post, pension, the works. Amma has already told half the colony.
Then Sonali called about her textile start-up. Four people, one rented room, no promise of salary after March. She wants me to run their online shop.
